title: Rental Turn and Make-Ready Checklist, Room by Room
metaDescription: A room-by-room rental turn checklist: move-out inspection, deposit documentation, trade sequencing between tenants, and make-ready standards that cut vacancy.
h1: Rental Turn and Make-Ready Checklist: A Room-by-Room Process Between Tenants
dek: A rental turn is the work between one tenant moving out and the next moving in: inspect and document, decide what is damage versus wear, sequence repairs, clean, and verify the unit is rent-ready. Done as a repeatable process with photos and a standard checklist, turns get faster, more consistent and easier to defend at deposit time.
keyTakeaways: Start the turn before move-out with a pre-move-out walkthrough, so parts and trades can be lined up for the day the unit is empty.
Document condition with dated photos and video at move-in and move-out, because deposit deductions depend on comparing the two.
Separate tenant damage from normal wear and tear room by room; only damage is generally chargeable against the deposit.
Sequence trades in order: repairs that make dust and mess first, then paint, then flooring, then final clean and inspection.
Use a written make-ready standard for the portfolio so every unit is turned to the same specification and finishes stay interchangeable.

sections.h2: What is a rental turn, and why does the process matter?
sections.body:
A turn, also called a make-ready, is everything that happens to a rental between the outgoing tenant handing back keys and the incoming tenant receiving them. It includes inspection, documentation, repairs, painting, cleaning, flooring work, pest treatment if needed, systems checks and a final rent-ready inspection.

Every day a unit sits empty is a day without rent while taxes, insurance, debt service and utilities continue. That makes the turn one of the few places where an owner has direct control over vacancy loss. The other reason the process matters is the deposit. Deductions from a security deposit generally must be itemized and supported, and the quality of the move-out documentation determines whether those deductions hold up.

The best turns are not improvised. They follow a written checklist, a standard finish specification and a sequence that the same crews repeat across units. That consistency matters most for owners with multiple doors: when every unit uses the same paint colors, flooring, fixtures and hardware, turn materials can be stocked, repairs are predictable and crews work faster.

This guide covers the process from pre-move-out through rent-ready, then works room by room through what to check and what commonly needs attention. Adapt it to your property types and local rules, especially on deposits, which are governed by state and sometimes local law.

sections.h2: How should you prepare before the tenant moves out?
sections.body:
The turn starts when notice is given, not when keys come back.

Schedule a pre-move-out walkthrough with the tenant where the lease and local law allow it. The goal is twofold. First, you see the unit's condition while there is still time to order parts, book trades and line up flooring or appliance replacements. Second, you give the tenant a chance to fix or clean things themselves, which can reduce deductions and disputes.

During that walkthrough, note likely work items: carpet that will need replacement, damaged doors, missing blinds, appliance problems the tenant has not reported, signs of pests or leaks. Take photos for your planning, but do not treat them as the final move-out record.

Send the tenant written move-out instructions covering cleaning expectations, key return, utility transfer, forwarding address and the deposit return process. A clear standard reduces arguments about what clean means.

Then build the turn plan. Line up materials with lead time, such as specific flooring, appliances, countertop repairs or replacement windows. Book the painter, cleaner and flooring installer with tentative dates. If the unit will need pest treatment, schedule it so it happens before cleaning and paint rather than after.

Finally, coordinate leasing. If the unit can be marketed before move-out, you can line up the next tenant to move in soon after the turn is complete. A turn that finishes before anyone is ready to rent the unit still loses rent.

sections.h2: How do you document condition for the security deposit?
sections.body:
Deposit disputes are won or lost on documentation. The basic principle is comparison: the move-out condition is judged against the move-in condition, less normal wear and tear for the length of the tenancy.

At move-in, record each room with dated photos and ideally a walkthrough video, plus a written condition checklist that the tenant signs or acknowledges where your process allows. Capture close-ups of existing scratches, stains, chips and wear so they cannot later be attributed to the tenant who did not cause them.

At move-out, repeat the same process in the same order, from the same angles where possible, once the tenant has removed their belongings. Photograph every room, including inside appliances, cabinets, closets, the garage, the yard and any storage areas. Note anything left behind.

For each deduction, keep:
- The move-in photo showing the original condition
- The move-out photo showing the damage
- The invoice, receipt or a reasonable documented cost for the repair
- A short explanation of why the item is damage rather than wear

State law sets the deadline for returning the deposit and itemizing deductions, and some cities add their own rules. Missing the deadline or failing to itemize properly can cost an owner the right to withhold anything, and in some places can lead to penalties. Know the rule where your property is and build it into the turn calendar.

sections.h2: What counts as damage versus normal wear and tear?
sections.body:
Normal wear and tear is the deterioration that comes from ordinary, reasonable use over time. Damage is harm beyond that, caused by accident, abuse or neglect. Exact definitions come from state law and case law, but the general pattern is consistent.

Commonly treated as normal wear:
- Light scuffs and minor marks on walls, and paint fading over a long tenancy
- A small number of nail holes from hanging pictures
- Carpet wear in traffic paths and slight matting
- Minor scratches on floors from normal furniture use
- Loose door handles, worn grout and faded blinds
- Small chips in fixtures from normal use

Commonly treated as damage:
- Large holes in walls or doors, and unauthorized paint colors
- Pet stains, odors, chewed trim and scratched doors
- Burns, large stains or tears in carpet
- Broken windows, blinds or fixtures
- Water damage from a tenant's neglect, such as an unreported leak they knew about
- Excessive dirt or grease that needs more than routine cleaning
- Missing items such as smoke detectors, appliances or keys

Age matters. Many jurisdictions expect deductions for items like carpet and paint to account for the item's remaining useful life, not its full replacement cost. Charging a tenant for new carpet that was already near the end of its life is a common source of disputes.

When in doubt, deduct conservatively and document carefully. A modest, well-supported deduction is usually better than a larger one that invites a challenge.

sections.h2: What is the right order of work during a turn?
sections.body:
Sequencing is where turns gain or lose days. The general rule is to do dirty and disruptive work first and clean and finish work last, so nothing finished gets damaged by a later trade.

A typical sequence:
- Trash-out and removal of anything the tenant left, plus a rough clean so crews can work
- Pest treatment if needed, since some treatments call for the unit to be unoccupied and undisturbed
- Repairs that create debris: drywall patching, door and trim replacement, cabinet repairs, plumbing and electrical fixes, window and screen repairs
- Systems work: HVAC filter change and service, water heater check, smoke and carbon monoxide alarm testing and replacement
- Paint, from ceilings to walls to trim, after patches are dry and sanded
- Flooring repair or replacement after paint so drips and ladders do not damage new floors
- Fixture and hardware installation, including blinds, outlet covers, light fixtures and door hardware
- Final deep clean: kitchen, appliances, bathrooms, windows, floors and fixtures
- Rekey or lock change
- Final rent-ready inspection against the checklist

Some trades can overlap. A cleaner can work on the kitchen while a handyman finishes the bedrooms, and exterior items like landscaping can proceed at the same time as interior work. What should not overlap is painting and flooring in the same room, or cleaning before dust-producing repairs are done.

The biggest schedule killers are waiting on materials and trades that cannot start until another trade finishes. That is why ordering materials during the pre-move-out window matters as much as the sequence itself.

Kitchens and bathrooms are where most turn costs and most tenant complaints originate, so they get the closest inspection.

Kitchen:
- Test every appliance through a full cycle: range burners and oven, refrigerator temperature, dishwasher fill and drain, microwave, disposal
- Inspect under the sink for leaks, water damage to the cabinet floor and the condition of supply and drain connections
- Check cabinet doors, hinges and drawer slides; tighten or replace
- Look at countertops for burns, cuts, chips and failing seams
- Check the backsplash and caulk at the counter and sink
- Test GFCI outlets and the range hood fan and light
- Clean grease from the hood filter, cabinets and walls
- Look for signs of pests in cabinets and behind appliances

Bathrooms:
- Run every faucet and the shower, checking pressure, temperature and drainage
- Flush the toilet, check for running, rocking and leaks at the base and supply
- Inspect caulk and grout at the tub, shower and floor; recaulk as needed
- Check the exhaust fan for operation and airflow
- Look for soft floors near the toilet and tub, which can indicate a leak
- Check for mold or mildew on ceilings, walls and around windows
- Test the GFCI outlet
- Replace the toilet seat, shower curtain rod or other worn items to the portfolio standard

In both rooms, small leaks are the priority. A slow drip under a sink or at a toilet base that goes unaddressed through a turn becomes a subfloor or cabinet replacement at the next one.

sections.h2: Room-by-room checklist: bedrooms, living areas, systems and exterior
sections.body:
Bedrooms and living areas:
- Patch holes and repaint to the portfolio standard color and sheen
- Inspect flooring for stains, tears, pet damage and loose transitions
- Test windows for operation, locks and screens; confirm bedroom windows open for egress
- Check closet doors, tracks and shelving
- Test all switches, outlets and light fixtures, replacing bulbs to a consistent type
- Replace damaged or missing blinds
- Check doors for holes, latching and hardware

Systems and safety:
- Replace the HVAC filter and confirm heating and cooling operate
- Check the water heater for leaks, venting and the relief valve discharge line
- Test smoke alarms and carbon monoxide alarms and replace any that are expired or missing, following local requirements for type and placement
- Check the electrical panel for proper labeling and any signs of overheating
- Confirm the dryer vent is clean and properly connected
- Check for gas smells and confirm appliance connections where present

Exterior and common areas:
- Inspect the roof, gutters and downspouts from the ground for obvious problems
- Check exterior doors, locks, weatherstripping and the doorbell
- Inspect decks, stairs and railings for loose or rotted components
- Clear trash, overgrowth and debris from the yard
- Check exterior lights and house numbers
- Inspect the garage door and opener, including the safety reverse

Finish with a rekey, a final clean and a rent-ready walkthrough by someone other than the person who did the work. A fresh set of eyes catches what the crew walked past.

sections.h2: How do you standardize turns across a rental portfolio?
sections.body:
Owners with more than a few doors get the most from standardization. The idea is to decide once what every unit should look like and stock the same materials everywhere.

A make-ready standard typically defines:
- One or two interior paint colors with a specified sheen for walls, trim and ceilings, so touch-ups match and partial repaints blend
- A standard flooring product, such as a durable luxury vinyl plank in main areas, chosen for water resistance and easy plank-by-plank repair
- Standard faucets, light fixtures, cabinet hardware, door hardware and blinds
- Standard appliances or a short approved list
- A standard lock or rekeyable cylinder system
- Minimum condition rules, such as when carpet is replaced rather than cleaned

The benefits compound. Materials can be bought in volume and kept on hand. Crews learn the standard and work faster. Repairs at one unit use the same parts as repairs at another. Tenants receive consistent quality, which supports renewals.

Upgrades made during a turn should move the unit toward the standard. If a unit still has carpet that wears out at every turn, replacing it with the standard hard-surface flooring is a turn cost that lowers future turn costs. The same logic applies to fixtures that break often or finishes that stain easily.

Finally, track turn data. Recording what each turn involved, how long it took and what it cost shows which units and which finishes drive repeat expense. Genstone's rental turn work for portfolio owners follows this kind of standard, because consistency is what lets a turn crew move quickly from one unit to the next.

faqs.q: How can I shorten the time between tenants?
faqs.a: Start before move-out. A pre-move-out walkthrough lets you order materials and book trades early. Market the unit before it is vacant if the lease allows showings. Use a portfolio-wide finish standard so materials are on hand. Sequence the work so dusty repairs come before paint and paint before flooring, and overlap trades in different rooms. Finally, have a different person do the final rent-ready inspection so callbacks do not delay move-in.

faqs.q: Can I charge a tenant for repainting the whole unit?
faqs.a: It depends on the condition and local law. Repainting after a normal tenancy is usually treated as the owner's expense because paint wears and fades with time. If the tenant caused damage beyond normal wear, such as large stains, smoke damage, unauthorized colors or extensive holes, a deduction may be appropriate. Many jurisdictions expect the deduction to reflect the paint's remaining useful life. Document the move-in and move-out condition with photos either way.

faqs.q: What should be in a rent-ready inspection?
faqs.a: A rent-ready inspection confirms the unit is clean, safe and fully functional before a new tenant arrives. Check every appliance, fixture, outlet, switch, window, door and lock. Test smoke and carbon monoxide alarms. Confirm heating, cooling and hot water work. Look for leaks under sinks and around toilets. Confirm the unit is clean, including inside appliances and cabinets. Take a dated photo set, which also becomes the next tenant's move-in documentation.

faqs.q: Should I replace carpet with hard flooring during a turn?
faqs.a: In many rentals, yes, when the carpet is due for replacement anyway. Durable hard-surface flooring such as luxury vinyl plank generally resists stains and pet damage better, cleans faster at the next turn and can often be repaired plank by plank. Some owners keep carpet in bedrooms for comfort or local tenant preference. The key is making the choice as part of a portfolio standard, not unit by unit at each turn.
